definition: Meritocratic means rewarding ability and achievement rather than wealth or birth.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word meritocratic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know meritocratic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The climbing gym is quietly meritocratic: route-setters are chosen from whoever tops the monthly competition, members and staff alike.
An open contest lets anyone enter — a low bar that stops far short of meritocratic, since the door can be open while connections still pick the winner.
A fair process bans cheating and favoritism, but it stops short of meritocratic until one more thing is true: that measured ability is what actually decides.

Merit-based is the plain, everyday label for the same idea: rewards follow demonstrated ability. Meritocratic means nothing more, but it is the analyst's word — the one essays use to characterize a whole system of exams, promotions, or admissions. Choose by register; the meaning is shared.

Evenhanded means playing no favorites — every entrant faces the same treatment and the same scrutiny. Meritocratic goes further and names what decides once favoritism is gone: measured ability and achievement. A coin flip is perfectly evenhanded, but only a contest of skill can be meritocratic.

The constitution's drafters argued for months over what kind of democracy theirs would be.
Meritocratic means rewarding ability and achievement rather than wealth or birth.
The astronomy club's telescope time is allocated on meritocratic terms — the best observation proposal wins the dark-sky weekend, whether it comes from a professor or a ninth grader.

Meritocratic is more precise than 'fair' because fairness only promises no cheating; a meritocratic system goes further and names what does decide — measured ability and achievement, rather than wealth, birth, or friends in the right rooms.
Meritocratic evaluates systems — exams, promotions, auditions — so it lives in essays and editorials.
'Fair' praises the absence of cheating; meritocratic makes the stronger claim that ability alone decides.

Keep its unit-mates straight by their first roots: a plutocratic system answers to wealth, a theocratic one to religious authority, an oligarchic one to a small circle — and a meritocratic one, at least on paper, to skill.

For decades the Halvorsen Symphony hired by audition-plus-interview, and somehow the winners kept being students of the same three teachers.
The reform was simple: a screen.
Candidates now play behind a curtain, identified by number, and the committee ranks what it hears and nothing else.
Supporters call the new process meritocratic in the strict sense — the job goes to demonstrated ability, measured note by note, rather than to pedigree or connections.
The first season under the screen, two of the five seats went to players no committee member had ever heard of.
One violinist put it plainly: 'The curtain doesn't care who your teacher was.'
